lesson.menu_title: How Do You Evaluate Your Team?
lesson.menu_desc: The question that cost you a role, answered properly -- and the twelve-month agenda behind it -- 38 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 8 -- How Do You Evaluate Your Team?
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Fernando Meneghelli Bottura | Lesson 8 -- How Do You Evaluate Your Team?

listenings.text: How do I evaluate a finance team. Three things, and they are always the same three. One, does the number arrive on the day it was promised. Two, is it right the first time, because a number that has to be corrected costs more credibility than a number that is late. And three, and this is the one that separates a good controller from a good business partner, does the business go to that person for advice before the decision, or after it. The first two I can measure from a calendar and an error log. The third one I cannot measure at all, so I ask. I ask the commercial director who he calls when he is putting a pitch together, and if my controller's name does not come up in a year, that tells me everything. And notice what is not on that list. Hours. I have never once evaluated anybody on hours, and I would not join a company that did.

The twelve month question is the one candidates prepare least and it is the one we care most about, because it is the only part of the interview that is about us rather than about them. A weak answer is a list of intentions. I will assess the team, I will review the processes, I will build relationships. Everybody says that and it tells me nothing. A strong answer has dates in it. By the end of the first month I will have met all four direct reports individually and I will have sat in on one close. By the end of the quarter I will have decided which of the three systems we keep. This time next year we will be closing in five days rather than nine. That last sentence is the one I write down, because it is a commitment, it is measurable, and it means the person has already understood what is broken here.

extra_audio.text: Sofia asks Fernando how he evaluates a finance team. Fernando gives three criteria and says the third one is the hardest. Fernando explains how he measures the third criterion without a report. Sofia asks what his first twelve months here would look like. Fernando answers with dates rather than intentions.

reading.rtitle: The two questions every CFO interview turns on
paras: There are two questions in a CFO process that decide more than all the technical ones put together. The first is how you evaluate a team. The second is what your first twelve months would look like. They are asked in almost every process, and they are the two that candidates prepare least, because they feel like soft questions and they are not.

The first one is a test of criteria. Anyone can say they look for accuracy and speed. What a panel is listening for is whether the criteria are measurable, whether the candidate knows which of them cannot be measured, and what they do about that. The answer that works names three things, admits which one resists measurement, and says how it is checked anyway.

The second is a test of understanding. A weak answer is a list of verbs with no dates: assess the team, review the processes, build relationships. It is not wrong, it is empty, and every candidate says it. A strong answer attaches a date to each commitment, and at least one of those commitments is a number that somebody could hold the candidate to a year later.

There is a reason panels weigh these so heavily. Technical depth is verifiable from a CV and two references. Judgement about people, and the willingness to commit to something measurable in front of strangers, are visible only in the room. That is what the forty minutes are actually for.
reading.source: Adapted from executive search practice notes

gist.prompt: What is the main point of this text?
choices: Technical questions decide most CFO interviews and should be prepared first.
Two apparently soft questions carry the most weight, because they show judgement and commitment that a CV cannot.
Panels prefer candidates who avoid committing to measurable targets too early.

items: Candidates usually prepare these two questions carefully.
The text says these are the two they prepare LEAST, because they feel like soft questions.
A good answer about evaluating a team admits that one criterion cannot be measured.
It names three things, admits which one resists measurement, and says how it is checked anyway.
Listing verbs such as assess, review and build is described as wrong.
The text says it is not wrong -- it is empty, and every candidate says it.
A strong twelve-month answer contains at least one number somebody could hold you to.
That is exactly what the text says a strong answer attaches to its commitments.
Panels weigh these questions because technical depth cannot be checked any other way.
The opposite: technical depth IS verifiable from a CV and references, which is why the room is used for the other thing.
